pos: n. (an abbey on the Dart in Devon, Benedictine from 1018, Cistercian from 1147, dissolved 1539, and rebuilt on its own medieval foundations between 1907 and 1938)
etymology: Old English bucca, a buck or stag, with fasten or faesten, a stronghold — the deer's stronghold on the river Dart.
biblical_def: Buckfast is the one English abbey whose church was raised twice. Founded about 1018, it became Savigniac and then Cistercian, was dissolved in 1539, and its stones were quarried for two centuries until nothing of the church stood above ground. In 1882 a community of French Benedictines expelled from their own country bought the site, uncovered the medieval foundations, and from 1907 built a new church on them — a handful of monks laying the stone themselves, never more than six at a time, finishing in 1938. Whatever a Reformed reader makes of the community, the act answers a text exactly. “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12), and the title that follows is the point of the whole passage: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12). Nehemiah's word to a demoralised city has the same shape — “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — and the promise underneath both is God's own: “I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old” (Amo 9:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restore as to return to a former state, to repair, to rebuild; and breach as the act of breaking, a gap, an opening made by breaking.
webster_full: RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former owner. To bring back to a former good state; to repair; to rebuild.
BREACH, n. The act of breaking, or state of being broken; a rupture; a break; a gap; the space between the severed parts of a solid body parted by violence.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or ground-work of any thing; that on which any thing stands, and by which it is supported.
WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; uncultivated.
ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.
scriptures: And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Amo 9:11
In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
Isa 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
corruption_summary: The one English abbey rebuilt on its own foundations, four centuries after it was pulled down.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near this entry is the sentimental reading of restoration — the idea that putting a building back is the same as recovering what it was for. Isaiah's promise is to a people, and the waste places are rebuilt by men whose fast God has accepted; the chapter spends its first half demolishing a religion of observance without mercy. A rebuilt church that does not “deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) has repaired a wall and nothing else.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's restoring work runs through ordinary men laying actual stone, and that he takes the credit for it. “will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen” (Amo 9:11) is quoted by James at the Jerusalem council and applied to the ingathering of the Gentiles — the rebuilding that matters is of a people, and buildings are at best its sign.
roots_summary: Old English bucca faesten, the buck's stronghold; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; Hebrew perets (H6556), a breach; Hebrew qum (H6965), to raise up; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste or ruin.
roots_lines: Old English bucca + faesten — the stronghold by the deer ford.
Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17).
Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, a gap; “The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12).
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to raise up; “and I will raise up his ruins” (Amo 9:11).
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste place, a ruin; “And they shall build the old wastes” (Isa 61:4).
usage: “thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12) — literally true at Buckfast.
“they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4) — the prophet's word for a quarried site.
“that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17) — the motive that is not vanity.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Devon, founded 1278 by Amicia countess of Devon; after the dissolution it became the house of Sir Francis Drake)
etymology: Old English bocland, book-land — land held by written charter rather than by folk custom.
biblical_def: Buckland was founded in 1278 by Amicia, countess of Devon, one of the last Cistercian houses established in England. It was surrendered in 1541, sold to Sir Richard Grenville, and in 1581 bought by Sir Francis Drake, who turned the abbey church itself into a dwelling — the nave floored across, a hall and chambers inside the walls, the tower a stair. The house still stands and is still called Buckland Abbey, and a man may walk through a Cistercian church that has been a sea captain's parlour for four hundred years. Jeremiah's lament over a conquered Jerusalem is the text, and it is not comfortable for either side of the Reformation argument: “Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2). Moses had warned Israel about the opposite danger, of receiving “houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not” (Deu 6:11) and forgetting who gave them. Buckland is both warnings in one building: a house lost by those who misused it, and gained by men who did not build it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; and alien as a foreigner, one born in or belonging to another country.
webster_full: INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession or in course of law; an estate which a man has by descent.
ALIEN, n. A foreigner; one born in or belonging to another country; one who is not a denizen or entitled to the privileges of a citizen.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country. One of another town, city, state or province in the same nation.
DWELLING, n. Habitation; place of residence; abode.
scriptures: Lam 5:2
Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens.
Deu 6:11
And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;
Deu 6:12
Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.
Psa 24:1
A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
corruption_summary: A Cistercian church with a sea captain's hall built inside it, and the two warnings that meet in one building.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the transfer of church property into private hands as the real engine of the English dissolution — a reform whose doctrine was often sound and whose beneficiaries were courtiers. It will not do for a Protestant dictionary to pretend otherwise. Moses foresaw the spiritual danger of such a windfall precisely: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage” (Deu 6:12).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no title to land is absolute, because “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein” (Psa 24:1). Monks held Buckland on that condition and lost it; Drake held it on the same condition and so do its present trustees. Book-land is still only book-land.
roots_summary: Old English bocland, land held by charter; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew zur (H2114), a stranger; Hebrew nokri (H5237), a foreigner; Hebrew melo (H4393), fulness.
roots_lines: Old English boc + land — land conveyed by a written book or charter.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; “Our inheritance is turned to strangers” (Lam 5:2).
Hebrew nokri (H5237) — a foreigner, an alien; “our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2).
Hebrew chaphar (H2658) — to dig; “and wells digged, which thou diggedst not” (Deu 6:11).
Hebrew melo (H4393) — fulness, that which fills; “and the fulness thereof” (Psa 24:1).
usage: “our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2) — said in 1541 and meant literally.
“beware lest thou forget the LORD” (Deu 6:12) — the warning to the man who inherits.
“The earth is the LORD'S” (Psa 24:1) — the only deed that is final.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in east Devon, founded 1201 by William Brewer as a daughter of Forde)
etymology: Old English personal name Duduc or Dunnuc with wella, a spring or well — the spring of Duduc.
biblical_def: Dunkeswell was founded in 1201 by William Brewer, the great royal administrator, as a daughter of Forde, and he was buried in its church. Nothing of the abbey survives but fragments in a field and a Victorian parish church built partly from its stone. The name is the lasting thing, and it is a well. Wells are among the plainest and most contested objects in Scripture: Isaac's first act in the land was that he “digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them” (Gen 26:18), and he gave them back their old names. That is what a reformation is — not the invention of a new spring but the reopening of one that was deliberately filled in. The prophet turns the figure to salvation itself: “Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation” (Isa 12:3). And our Lord moves the well inside the man: “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14) — which is the one well that cannot be stopped by an enemy or quarried for a village church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines well as a spring, a fountain, and a pit or cylindrical hole sunk into the earth to the water; and spring as a fountain of water, an issue of water from the earth.
webster_full: WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; the issuing of water from the earth. A pit or cylindrical hole, sunk perpendicularly into the earth to such a depth as to reach a supply of water.
SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth.
DRAW, v.t. To pull along; to haul; to cause to move forward by force applied in advance of the thing moved.
THIRST, n. That uneasiness or pain occasioned by want of drink; a painful sensation of the throat or fauces.
scriptures: And Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham: and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them.
Isa 12:3
Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
corruption_summary: An abbey named for a spring, and the one well that no enemy can stop and no quarryman can carry away.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the hewn cistern — the substitute supply a man digs for himself because the spring is not under his control. Jeremiah states the double charge without softening it: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). A religious institution is a cistern by nature; it stores what it did not make, and it leaks. The fault is not in having one but in drinking from it as though it were the spring.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaac's method. He did not seek new water; he reopened his father's wells and called them by their old names, and that is the whole temper of a true reformation. “and he called their names after the names by which his father had called them” (Gen 26:18) is a rebuke to novelty and to antiquarianism at once: the names were old, but the digging was work done now.
roots_summary: Old English wella, a spring; Hebrew beer (H875), a well; Hebrew mayan (H4599), a spring or fountain; Hebrew bor (H953), a cistern or pit; Greek pege (G4077), a spring.
roots_lines: Old English wella — a spring, a welling-up of water.
Hebrew beer (H875) — a well, a dug pit for water; “the wells of water, which they had digged” (Gen 26:18).
Hebrew mayan (H4599) — a spring, a fountain; “out of the wells of salvation” (Isa 12:3).
Hebrew bor (H953) — a cistern, a hewn pit; “hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns” (Jer 2:13).
Greek pege (G4077) — a spring, a well; “a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14).
usage: “the Philistines had stopped them” (Gen 26:18) — what every generation does to the last one's wells.
“with joy shall ye draw water” (Isa 12:3) — the manner, not only the fact.
“that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13) — the verdict on every substitute.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey near Axminster in Devon, founded 1247 by Reginald and William de Mohun; one of the last of the order's English foundations)
etymology: Old English niwan hamm, the new enclosure or river-meadow — the new homestead by the Axe.
biblical_def: Newenham was founded in 1247 by the brothers Reginald and William de Mohun, a daughter of Beaulieu, and it was among the last Cistercian houses planted in England — more than a century after the great wave of the eleven-forties, when the order's first fervour was long spent and its best land taken. It was never rich, and it was dissolved with the rest. A latecomer among houses has an obvious text, and it is a parable about wages. The householder goes out “about the eleventh hour” (Mat 20:6) and finds men standing idle, and at the reckoning “when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9) — the same as those who had borne the heat of the day. The parable is not about fairness in employment. It is about the murmuring of the early-hired against a generosity that costs them nothing, and it ends where the kingdom always ends: “So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hire as to procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price; and penny as an ancient denarius, a Roman coin, the eighth part of an ounce.
webster_full: HIRE, v.t. To procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price, or for a stipulated or reasonable equivalent.
PENNY, n. An ancient English silver coin; but now an imaginary money of account. In Scripture, the denarius, a Roman coin.
IDLE, a. Not employed; unoccupied with business; inactive; doing nothing.
LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan.
MURMUR, v.i. To utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice; to utter sullen discontent.
scriptures: Mat 20:6
And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and saith unto them, Why stand ye here all the day idle?
Mat 20:9
And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny.
And when they had received it, they murmured against the goodman of the house,
So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
corruption_summary: One of the last Cistercian houses in England, and the parable about being hired at the eleventh hour.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the murmur of the early-hired, which is the oldest grievance inside the church and the hardest to name as sin because it dresses as justice. “they murmured against the goodman of the house” (Mat 20:11) is Matthew's word for men who had received exactly what they agreed to. Seniority, long service and early conversion generate a claim that the gospel does not recognise, and a late-founded house, like a late convert, is a standing provocation to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that grace is not wages, and the parable is placed immediately after the rich young ruler and Peter's question about what the apostles would get. “for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16) closes the door on any arithmetic of merit. The eleventh-hour man does not receive less, and the first-hour man is not cheated; he is simply not the standard by which God gives.
roots_summary: Old English niwan hamm, the new enclosure; Greek misthoomai (G3409), to hire; Greek denarion (G1220), a penny; Greek argos (G692), idle; Greek gogguzo (G1111), to murmur.
roots_lines: Old English niwe + hamm — the new river-meadow enclosure.
Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “about the eleventh hour” (Mat 20:6).
Greek argos (G692) — inactive, idle; “found others standing idle” (Mat 20:6).
Greek denarion (G1220) — a denarius, a day's wage; “received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9).
Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to mutter, to murmur; “they murmured against the goodman of the house” (Mat 20:11).
usage: “Why stand ye here all the day idle?” (Mat 20:6) — the question put to latecomers.
“received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9) — the scandal of the parable.
“So the last shall be first” (Mat 20:16) — the order of the kingdom.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Somerset, founded 1198 by William de Roumare; its cloister buildings survive almost entire because the site was used as a farm)
etymology: Old English clif, a cliff or steep bank — the house under the hill, Latinised Vallis Florida, the flowering valley.
biblical_def: Cleeve was founded in 1198 by William de Roumare and called in its charters Vallis Florida. The church was pulled down after the dissolution, but the claustral range — refectory with its painted walls and carved roof, dormitory, chapter house, gatehouse — survives more completely than at any other English Cistercian site, for the ordinary reason that a farmer needed barns and chambers and the buildings were useful. What was consecrated was destroyed; what was merely domestic was kept, because it could be put to common work. Paul's figure of the great house is exactly this: “in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour” (2Ti 2:20). The apostle is not writing about buildings but about men in a congregation, and the conclusion he draws is practical and hopeful: “If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2Ti 2:21). The vessel is not fixed by its material.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vessel as any hollow utensil for holding liquors or other things, and in Scripture a person; and refectory as a room of refreshment, an eating room.
webster_full: VESSEL, n. A cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things. In Scripture, a person; as a chosen vessel.
REFECTORY, n. A room of refreshment; properly, a hall or apartment in convents and monasteries, where a moderate repast is taken.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery. A peristyle; a piazza; an arcade.
HONOR, n. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation. Dignity; exalted rank or place.
PURGE, v.t. To cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign or superfluous.
scriptures: But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.
Rom 9:21
Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
corruption_summary: The abbey whose church was destroyed and whose kitchens survive, because the useful was spared and the sacred was not.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sacred-and-secular split that the fate of Cleeve so neatly illustrates — the assumption that a building set apart for worship is holy in a way that a dining hall is not, and that therefore the one must go and the other may stay. Scripture consecrates persons, not masonry. “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” (Rom 9:21) makes the distinction God's to assign and not the material's to claim.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that usefulness to the Master is the real category of honour, and it is attainable: “meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2Ti 2:21). The refectory at Cleeve stands because it was useful; it would be a better sermon still if the congregation drew the obvious inference about themselves.
roots_summary: Old English clif, a steep bank; Greek skeuos (G4632), a vessel; Greek time (G5092), honour; Greek ekkathairo (G1571), to cleanse out; Greek euchrestos (G2173), useful.
roots_lines: Old English clif — a cliff, a steep slope.
Greek skeuos (G4632) — a vessel, an implement; “vessels of gold and of silver” (2Ti 2:20).
Greek time (G5092) — honour, value; “and some to honour, and some to dishonour” (2Ti 2:20).
Greek ekkathairo (G1571) — to cleanse thoroughly; “If a man therefore purge himself from these” (2Ti 2:21).
Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — of baked clay; “this treasure in earthen vessels” (2Co 4:7).
usage: “but also of wood and of earth” (2Ti 2:20) — the range that survived at Cleeve.
“he shall be a vessel unto honour” (2Ti 2:21) — the promotion on offer.
“of the same lump” (Rom 9:21) — the clay has no claim either way.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Sussex, founded 1176 by Alured de St Martin; its abbot searched Germany for the captive King Richard I in 1193)
etymology: From Robert de St Martin, with bridge; the Latin name was Pons Roberti, Robert's bridge over the Rother.
biblical_def: Robertsbridge was founded in 1176 by Alured de St Martin and his wife, a daughter of Boxley. Its best moment came in 1193, when Richard I was held prisoner by the emperor Henry VI and the government of England sent two men to find him: the abbot of Robertsbridge and the abbot of Boxley. They travelled through Germany until they came to him at Ochsenfurt, and they stayed with him. Chroniclers record it briefly and without ornament, which is the right way to record it. The duty they discharged is commanded of every Christian in a verse too easily read as sentiment: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3). The remembering is not emotional. It is the kind that gets on a horse. The church at Jerusalem did the same for Peter in the only way then open to it, for “Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him” (Act 12:5), and the Psalmist settles the question of whether God notices: “For the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners” (Psa 69:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines captive as a prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war; and ransom as the money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave.
webster_full: CAPTIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy; one taken and held in confinement.
RANSOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.
BONDS, n. Chains; fetters; imprisonment; captivity.
ADVERSITY, n. An event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress.
REMEMBER, v.t. To have in the mind an idea which had been in the mind before, and which recurs without effort.
scriptures: Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Act 12:5
Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him.
For the LORD heareth the poor, and despiseth not his prisoners.
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
corruption_summary: The abbey whose abbot rode across Germany to find a captive king, and the commandment that sent him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the substitution of feeling for visiting. “as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) requires an identification so complete that the free man reckons himself inside the cell, and that reckoning is tested by whether he goes. The medieval church institutionalised the duty in ransom orders and sometimes corrupted it into a trade; the modern church more often reduces it to awareness, which costs still less.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain terms of the judgement scene, where the King names the visit as done to himself: “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36). The prisoner in view is not necessarily innocent, and the text does not raise the question. Two abbots crossing the Rhine for a king who had taxed them to the bone understood the commandment better than most of their critics.
roots_summary: Latin Pons Roberti, Robert's bridge; Greek desmios (G1198), a prisoner in bonds; Greek mimnesko (G3403), to remember; Greek kakoucheo (G2558), to suffer adversity; Hebrew asir (H615), a prisoner.
roots_lines: Latin Pons Roberti — Robert's bridge, over the Sussex Rother.
Greek desmios (G1198) — one bound, a prisoner; “Remember them that are in bonds” (Heb 13:3).
Greek mimnesko (G3403) — to be mindful of, to remember.
Greek kakoucheo (G2558) — to maltreat, to suffer adversity; “them which suffer adversity” (Heb 13:3).
Hebrew asir (H615) — a prisoner, one bound; “and despiseth not his prisoners” (Psa 69:33).
usage: “as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3) — the reason the abbots went.
“prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him” (Act 12:5) — the other half of the duty.
“I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) — the King's own accounting.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Comminges, Gascony, founded 1136; its cloister was broken up and sold in the nineteenth century, and much of it now stands in New York)
etymology: Old French bonne font, the good spring, Latin Bonus Fons — the abbey of the good fountain.
biblical_def: Bonnefont-en-Comminges was founded in 1136 in the foothills of the Pyrenees, a daughter of Morimond, and was suppressed at the French Revolution. Its buildings were quarried, and in the nineteenth century the marble cloister was taken apart and sold column by column: some capitals went into a local garden, others to a bath-house, a great many to dealers, and from the dealers to George Grey Barnard and so to The Cloisters in New York, where a reconstructed Bonnefont arcade now overlooks the Hudson. A house of prayer sold in pieces to the highest bidders has one inescapable text, and it is the most solemn in the Psalter: “They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture” (Psa 22:18). Micah had pronounced the sentence on a sanctuary that had become a trade: “Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps” (Mic 3:12), and he names the reason without flinching — priests who “teach for hire” (Mic 3:11) and prophets who “divine for money” (Mic 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cloister as a peristyle or arcade, and a monastery; and dispersion as the act of scattering, the state of being scattered or separated into remote parts.
webster_full: CLOISTER, n. A peristyle; a piazza; an arcade. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns.
DISPERSION, n. The act of scattering or dispersing; the state of being scattered, or separated into remote parts.
ARCADE, n. A long or continued arch; a walk arched above.
CAPITAL, n. The uppermost part of a column, pillar or pilaster, serving as the head or crowning.
TRAFFIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
scriptures: They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.
Mic 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
Mic 3:12
Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest.
Act 8:20
But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
corruption_summary: A Pyrenean abbey sold capital by capital, and its cloister rebuilt above the Hudson.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the commodification of the sacred, which is not peculiar to revolutionaries or antiquarians: Micah lays it at the door of the clergy first. “The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money” (Mic 3:11) is a description of an establishment, and the sentence on it is that the mountain of the house becomes a wooded height. Bonnefont was sold because it had already been emptied.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Peter's refusal to let the gift of God enter the market at all: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). The stones of a cloister may lawfully be bought and sold; what they were built to house may not, and the confusion of the two is the whole history of simony.
roots_summary: Old French bonne font, good spring; Hebrew chalaq (H2505), to divide or apportion; Hebrew goral (H1486), a lot; Hebrew mechir (H4242), a price or hire; Greek argurion (G694), silver or money.
roots_lines: Old French bonne font — the good spring, Latin Bonus Fons.
Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to divide, to apportion; “They part my garments among them” (Psa 22:18).
Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot, that which is cast; “and cast lots upon my vesture” (Psa 22:18).
Hebrew mechir (H4242) — a price, hire; “the priests thereof teach for hire” (Mic 3:11).
Greek argurion (G694) — silver, money; “may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20).
usage: “and cast lots upon my vesture” (Psa 22:18) — said over a marble cloister in pieces.
“and Jerusalem shall become heaps” (Mic 3:12) — the sentence, and its stated cause.
“Thy money perish with thee” (Act 8:20) — the only acceptable price.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Bigorre, Gascony, founded 1142; its name is Latin Scala Dei, the ladder of God)
etymology: Occitan escala Dieu, from Latin Scala Dei, the ladder of God — the house named for Jacob's dream.
biblical_def: L'Escaladieu was founded in 1142 in the valley of the Arros below the Pyrenees, a daughter of Morimond, and became the burial place of the counts of Bigorre. Its name is a sermon: Scala Dei, the ladder of God, taken from the stone at Bethel where “he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12). Medieval monasticism loved the figure and built a whole literature of ascent on it — steps of humility, rungs of contemplation, the cloister as a ladder from earth to heaven. Our Lord takes the same image and puts something else at the centre of it. To Nathanael he says “Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51). The ladder is not a discipline, and it is not the cloister. It is a person, and the traffic on it moves in both directions because he came down before anyone went up. Jacob's own response remains the best one: “Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ladder as a frame of wood consisting of two side pieces connected by rounds, used for ascending; and ascend as to move upwards, to mount, to go up, to rise.
webster_full: LADDER, n. A frame of wood, consisting of two side pieces, connected by rounds inserted in them at suitable distances, and thus forming steps, by which persons may ascend a building.
ASCEND, v.i. To move upwards; to mount; to go up; to rise, whether in air or water, or upon a material object.
DESCEND, v.i. To move or pass from a higher to a lower place; to move, come or go downward; to fall; to sink.
VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; actual sight. Something imaginary; the production of fancy. In Scripture, a revelation from God.
BETHEL, n. The house of God; a place of worship.
scriptures: And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Joh 1:51
And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
corruption_summary: An abbey named the Ladder of God, and the question of what stands on the bottom rung.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the ladder of ascent as a programme — the conviction that a graded discipline carries a man upward toward God, with the cloister as the apparatus. Jacob did not climb his ladder. He was asleep at the bottom of it, running from a brother he had cheated, and the traffic on the stair was angelic and downward first. Any spirituality that puts the climber at the centre has reversed the dream.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the identification our Lord makes of himself with the ladder, which settles the direction of all genuine mediation. Jacob's fear is also instructive and is usually skipped: “How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen 28:17). A man who meets God where he did not expect him is frightened before he is comforted, and a religion that never frightens anyone has probably not met him.
roots_summary: Latin Scala Dei, the ladder of God; Hebrew sullam (H5551), a ladder or stairway; Hebrew malak (H4397), a messenger or angel; Hebrew sha-ar (H8179), a gate; Greek anabaino (G305), to go up.
roots_lines: Latin Scala Dei — the ladder of God, the abbey's name.
Hebrew sullam (H5551) — a ladder, a stairway; “behold a ladder set up on the earth” (Gen 28:12).
Hebrew malak (H4397) — a messenger, an angel; “the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12).
Hebrew sha-ar (H8179) — a gate; “and this is the gate of heaven” (Gen 28:17).
Greek anabaino (G305) — to ascend, to go up; “the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51).
usage: “and the top of it reached to heaven” (Gen 28:12) — the name the abbey took.
“and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16) — the honest half of the dream.
“upon the Son of man” (Joh 1:51) — where the ladder turns out to stand.

pos: n. (a Cistercian nunnery in Hainaut, founded 1228; source of the Beaupre Antiphonary, one of the great illuminated choirbooks of the thirteenth century)
etymology: Old French beau pre, the fair meadow, Latin Bellum Pratum — the abbey of the beautiful pasture.
biblical_def: Beaupre-sur-la-Dendre in Hainaut was a house of Cistercian nuns founded in 1228, and between 1286 and 1290 its sisters commissioned and used a four-volume antiphonary — the book of sung offices — whose illumination is among the finest produced in the Low Countries. The volumes are now divided between the Walters Art Museum and other collections. A convent named Bellum Pratum which spent four hundred years singing from such a book sits under two texts at once. The first is the shepherd psalm, where “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters” (Psa 23:2) — and the making is not gentle in the Hebrew; it is a shepherd compelling sheep to rest. The second is Paul's instruction for what a congregation is to do with such a book: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord” (Col 3:16). Singing is there a means of teaching, which is why the words must be true.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antiphon as the chant or alternate singing in choirs of cathedrals; and pasture as grass for the food of cattle, the food of cattle taken by grazing.
webster_full: ANTIPHON, n. The chant or alternate singing in choirs of cathedrals. A species of psalmody, when a congregation is divided into two parts, and each sings the verses alternately.
PASTURE, n. Grass for the food of cattle; the food of cattle taken by grazing. Ground covered with grass appropriated for the food of cattle.
PSALMODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs; the singing of psalms in public worship.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To adorn with colored pictures or letters, as a manuscript.
MEADOW, n. A tract of low land appropriated to the culture of grass for hay.
scriptures: Psa 23:2
He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
corruption_summary: A convent called the fair meadow, a famous choirbook, and the rule that singing is teaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near a great choirbook is the slow separation of music from meaning — the point at which a congregation sings because the sound is beautiful and no longer attends to what the words assert. Paul forestalls it by making song a mode of instruction: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). The modern form is identical and is not confined to high liturgy; a chorus repeated forty times teaches as surely as an antiphon, and teaches whatever it says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing of the heart and the words: “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). Neither half may be dropped. The Beaupre sisters had the book; the question Scripture puts to them and to every choir after them is whether the melody was in the heart, and that question no manuscript can answer.
roots_summary: Old French beau pre, fair meadow; Hebrew naveh (H5116), a pasture or habitation; Hebrew deshe (H1877), green grass; Greek psalmos (G5568), a psalm; Greek ado (G103), to sing.
roots_lines: Old French beau pre — the fair meadow, Latin Bellum Pratum.
Hebrew naveh (H5116) — a pasture, a habitation; “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures” (Psa 23:2).
Hebrew menuchah (H4496) — a resting place, quietness; “he leadeth me beside the still waters” (Psa 23:2).
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song sung to accompaniment; “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).
Greek ado (G103) — to sing; “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19).
usage: “He maketh me to lie down” (Psa 23:2) — the shepherd compels the rest.
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Col 3:16) — the condition of true singing.
“Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4) — the manner of approach.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Sambre in Hainaut, Cistercian from 1147; burnt by French revolutionary troops in 1794 and never rebuilt)
etymology: Old French aulne, the alder tree, Latin Alna — the abbey among the alders on the Sambre.
biblical_def: Aulne was an ancient foundation, traditionally seventh-century, which took the Cistercian rule in 1147 and became one of the great houses of the Low Countries, with a library of thousands of volumes and a church of the first rank. In 1794 troops of the French Republic burnt it. The monks were dispersed, the library destroyed or scattered, and the roofless shell beside the river is what remains. The Psalter contains the lament written for exactly this, and it is worth quoting at length because it refuses to be vague: “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7). What follows is the part that is hardest and truest: “We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long” (Psa 74:9). The psalm does not resolve into reassurance. It appeals to God's own name and ancient acts and leaves the question open, which is the honest posture of a church under a state that has decided against it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sanctuary as a sacred place, a place of protection; and sacrilege as the crime of violating or profaning sacred things, the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religion.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, called the Holy of Holies. Hence, a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; or the alienating to laymen or to common purposes what has been appropriated or consecrated to religious persons or uses.
PROFANE, v.t. To violate any thing sacred, or treat it with abuse, irreverence, obloquy or contempt.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; desert; uninhabited; laid waste.
ALDER, n. A tree of the genus Alnus, usually growing in wet lands.
scriptures: Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
Psa 74:8
They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.
Psa 74:9
We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.
Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily.
corruption_summary: A great Belgian abbey burnt by the Republic in 1794, and the psalm that refuses to make it tidy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the revolutionary state's claim to dispose of the church — a claim that calls itself liberation and proceeds by fire. The psalmist describes the method with a precision that fits 1794 as well as it fits 587 BC: “They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land” (Psa 74:8). The intention is named as well as the act, and it is an intention of the heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lawfulness of the unresolved complaint. “Arise, O God, plead thine own cause” (Psa 74:22) is a prayer that hands the matter back where it belongs, and it does not pretend the loss was small or the timing understood. A Protestant reader who would not have wept over a Cistercian library should notice that the psalm was given to the whole church, and that the men who burnt Aulne went on to burn the Protestant chapels too.
roots_summary: Latin Alna, the alder; Hebrew miqdash (H4720), a sanctuary; Hebrew esh (H784), fire; Hebrew chalal (H2490), to profane; Hebrew rib (H7378), to plead a cause.
roots_lines: Latin Alna — the alder, the tree of the Sambre banks.
Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a sanctuary, a holy place; “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7).
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to pollute; “they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name” (Psa 74:7).
Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn; “they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land” (Psa 74:8).
Hebrew rib (H7378) — to contend, to plead a cause; “Arise, O God, plead thine own cause” (Psa 74:22).
usage: “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7) — the Sambre valley, 1794.
“neither is there among us any that knoweth how long” (Psa 74:9) — the sentence that is not tidied up.
“plead thine own cause” (Psa 74:22) — where the matter is left.
